title: The divine dance
hookLine: Greek fathers described the three persons as dwelling in one another, like a round dance

cards: A circle of people at a wedding, arms on each other's shoulders, stepping left, then right. Nobody in the circle is the center. Nobody leads for long.
If one person stops, the whole ring feels it. And if you ask where the dance is, you can't point to any one dancer. It's in all of them, and between them.
Some Christian writers have reached for exactly that picture to talk about God. Not a ruler on a throne, not a triangle on a whiteboard: a ring of movement.
Like every picture of the Trinity, it falls short, but in a lively way.

teach.h: I IN THE FATHER, THE FATHER IN ME.
teach.b: Perichoresis. Greek Christian writers used it for something Jesus says in John's Gospel. He asks Philip: "Believest thou not that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?"
Not beside. In. Later, praying for his friends, he widens it: "as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us."

Teachers in the Greek-speaking churches, John of Damascus among them, used perichoresis to name that mutual in-ness: Father, Son and Spirit each dwelling in the others, without blurring into one another and without being split apart.

teach.h: EACH AT HOME IN THE OTHERS.
teach.b: Each makes room for the others, and is at home in them. Now the dance. In English the word sounds like choreography, and some modern writers have run with that: God as a round dance, three persons moving in one movement.
Others point out that the root is about going around and making room, not dancing, and would rather keep the picture loose. Both agree on what it's for. God is not a lonely thing.
Before there was anything, Christians say, there was already giving and receiving, love going out and coming back. And then the prayer: that they also may be one in us.

teach.h: A RING WITH A GAP HELD OPEN.
teach.b: The circle has a gap, and the gap is held open. Christians differ on how far to push that. Orthodox teachers speak boldly of people being drawn into God's life; others put it more carefully.
Either way, the ring in this picture is not closed.

how: Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant theologians use the word perichoresis when they teach about the Trinity, and some churches have icons and hymns that speak of the three persons dwelling in one another.

s: perichoresis means the three persons blur into one
each dwells in the others without blurring into one another and without being split apart.
in John's Gospel, Jesus prays that his friends may be one in us
"as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us."
everyone agrees the word comes from the Greek for dance
some writers hear a dance in it; others say its root is about going around and making room.

games.q: you want a picture of God that says the three persons are in one another, not just side by side. which do you pick?
o: a ring of people moving as one.
games.why: some Christian writers reach for a round dance: nobody is the center, and the dance is in all of them at once. they also say every picture falls short.

practice: If you can, stand and turn slowly all the way around, a full breath for each step; if not, trace a slow circle with one hand. As you turn, think of the people who make room for you, and the people you make room for.
If you pray, say the line from John, that they also may be one in us; if not, let the circle be the whole of it.

wordCard.voice: Perichoresis. The persons of the Trinity dwelling in one another, each making room for the others: some say, like a dance.

orig.note: Greek: dwelling in one another, making room. Greek Christian writers used it for the Trinity.

carryVoice: Your line: god is a dance. A ring, with a gap held open. Go gently.
